summary: Describes the procedure for defining new DHCP options. It sets out rules so new options are consistent and well documented. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 2939.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2489 explains how to propose a new DHCP option. It requires review and publication before IANA assigns the option number.

subtitle: A procedure for defining and assigning new DHCP options.

tldr.problem: DHCP needed a coordinated process to review and document new options before their option numbers were assigned.
tldr.mechanism: An author documents an option, submits it for review, and receives an IANA option number when its specification is published as an RFC.

sections.title: What a DHCP Option Is
sections.content: DHCP passes configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network. The information is carried in tagged data items stored in the options field of a DHCP message; these items are also called options. RFC 2489 describes a process intended to coordinate option numbers, review technical correctness, and ensure complete published documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP messages contain numbered options that carry configuration information. This RFC sets a process for defining new options and assigning their numbers.

sections.title: Public and Private Option Ranges
sections.content: The RFC divides DHCP option numbers 1 through 254 into public options 1 through 127 and site-specific private-use options 128 through 254. Public options require review before IANA assigns a number. The number for a new public option is assigned when its specification is about to be published as an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Public options need review; private-use options are for site-specific use. A public option receives its number at RFC publication.

sections.title: Steps for a New Public Option
sections.content: The author drafts a specification with the option code marked To Be Determined, then submits it for review by the IESG, preferably through the DHC Working Group. If accepted, the specification is published as an RFC, either standards-track or non-standards-track. IANA assigns the option number at publication; the RFC says the option should not be used before then.
sections.plainLanguage: The author writes and submits a specification for review. If it is accepted and published as an RFC, IANA assigns its number.
